items.scene: A friend asks you to repeat another friend's private medical diagnosis to a coworker who is curious.
items.question: What should you do?
options: Share it because the coworker asked
Post it later if nobody objects
items.why_this_case_matters: This is a direct disclosure-boundary decision about a private fact and an outside audience.

items.scene: You already told someone a secret that was meant to stay private, and now the person is upset.
items.question: What is the main issue now?
options: Whether it was allowed to share
How to apologize and repair trust
How to make the secret sound less serious
Whether to tell even more people
items.why_this_case_matters: The boundary has already been crossed, so this unit should exit to repair.

items.scene: You are updating your online bio and want to leave out an embarrassing detail so you seem more polished.
items.question: Does this unit fit the main decision?
options: Yes, because it is about privacy boundaries
No, this is self-presentation, not disclosure
Yes, because it is about repairing harm
No, because it is only about role hierarchy
items.why_this_case_matters: This is a likely shortcut error: controlling image is not the same as deciding what may be disclosed.

items.scene: A parent wants to post that their child got a big award and include a private health detail because the news is positive and harmless.
items.question: What is the best judgment?
options: Share it because positive details are fine
Keep the health detail private unless the child agreed
Treat it as an apology issue
items.why_this_case_matters: A flattering detail can still be private, so the disclosure boundary still controls.
